enrichment.short_title: Setting aside statutory demand where Chancery cross-claim exceeds costs debt
key_facts: Ronald Popely served a statutory demand on his brother John for about £41,617 under a Crown Court costs order arising from document-access proceedings linked to Chancery litigation.
John had consolidated Chancery actions against Ronald claiming the same underlying relief and applied to set aside the statutory demand relying on that cross-demand.
A district judge dismissed the set-aside application under the summary r.6.5(1) procedure without giving reasons; a deputy High Court judge allowed John's appeal and set the demand aside.
Ronald appealed, arguing the pending Chancery claim was not a qualifying cross-demand and that setting aside would subvert the forthwith costs order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a deputy High Court judge's decision setting aside a bankruptcy statutory demand.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; statutory demand remains set aside; Ronald ordered to pay costs of £20,750.
enrichment.ratio: Under Insolvency Rules 1986 r.6.5(4)(a), a genuine cross-demand in pending litigation may justify setting aside a statutory demand based on an interlocutory costs order without subverting enforcement of that order; delay and impecuniosity are generally not matters for the set-aside stage unless they cast doubt on genuineness.

enrichment.short_title: CRHP appeal test for unduly lenient GMC suspension of Dr Solanke

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service Reform and Health Care Professions Act 2002

key_facts: Dr Olagbalekan Solanke admitted serious professional misconduct for a sexual relationship with patient Ms X and falsifying his birth certificate and CV to appear younger.
The GMC Professional Conduct Committee suspended him from the register for three months after he had already been off work for about six months.
The Council for the Regulation of Healthcare Professionals referred the sanction as unduly lenient under section 29 of the 2002 Act.

enrichment.short_title: Fort Road vehicular right of way over Wendy’s frontage

statutes_considered.title: National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949

key_facts: Mrs Worth claimed a vehicular right of way along Fort Road to Betchworth Fort, a chalet and caravan site she and her family had operated since the 1920s.

The judge found an express 1921 grant of a 12 foot 6 inch way and a prescriptive vehicular right over the turning area known as the V.

enrichment.short_title: NASS support for infirm asylum seeker with dependent children
key_facts: O, an HIV-positive Ugandan asylum seeker with two young children, received accommodation and subsistence from Haringey after leaving her home due to domestic violence.
Haringey accepted a section 21 National Assistance Act duty to O as an infirm destitute but argued NASS must fund the children.
Ouseley J held the whole family destitute and fully within the NASS scheme; the Court of Appeal largely agreed but refined the split of responsibility.
Neither section 21 nor Children Act provisions made family accommodation legally available so as to exclude section 95 destitution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review on allocation of asylum support between NASS and a local authority.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; family treated as destitute under section 95; local authority retains section 21 duty to mother while Secretary of State must support children as part of her household under section 122.
enrichment.ratio: Where an infirm destitute asylum seeker has dependent children, the family unit is destitute for section 95 if accommodation or essential needs are not legally available from other sources; section 21 covers the mother and section 122 displaces section 17 duties for children, with NASS funding the children's share in practice.

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe conviction for historic indecent assault on babysitting complainant
key_facts: The appellant was convicted by a 10-2 majority of indecent assault on Clare, aged 6 or 7, while babysitting around 1981-1983; counts 2-4 were left on the file.
Complaints were first made to police in September 2002, about twenty years after the alleged conduct.
The appellant was 16 at the time; sisters gave consistent accounts on counts 1 and 2 but diverged on later counts.
He received a three-year community rehabilitation order and five-year notification requirement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Where historic child indecent assault is alleged after long delay, courts should scrutinise evidence carefully; inconsistent jury verdicts between sisters whose accounts matched on the core conduct can render a conviction unsafe.

enrichment.short_title: Fairchild extended to self-employed exposure; no apportionment
key_facts: Mr Barker died of mesothelioma after asbestos exposure at John Summers steelworks (1960-1968), a six-week Graessers job (1958), and over twenty years of self-employed plastering.
The defendant accepted breach during the Summers employment but argued Fairchild did not apply where self-employment exposure might have caused the disease and sought apportionment.
Moses J awarded four-fifths of agreed damages after 20% contributory negligence for failure to take precautions while self-employed.
Medical evidence could not attribute disease to any particular exposure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from High Court judgment applying Fairchild in a multi-source asbestos exposure mesothelioma claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; employer remains fully liable for indivisible injury subject to contributory negligence reduction; no apportionment by exposure share.
enrichment.ratio: Fairchild applies where relevant self-employment exposure exists; fault during self-employment is addressed by contributory negligence, not exclusion of liability; mesothelioma remains an indivisible injury with concurrent tortfeasor joint and several liability and no Fairchild-specific apportionment.
legal_issues: Whether Fairchild requires all exposure to be tortious employment by others
Whether liability should be apportioned by material increase in risk
